analysis.one_liner: Phases out the federal exemption letting employers pay disabled workers below minimum wage.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to end subminimum wages for workers with disabilities won 52 cosponsors from both parties, but the House Education and Workforce Committee never acted on it and it died without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law currently lets employers with a special certificate pay workers whose earning capacity is impaired by disability, age, or injury less than the minimum wage. This bill would immediately stop issuing new certificates, require existing certificate holders to file annual plans for moving each worker into jobs paying at or above minimum wage, and repeal the entire program six years after enactment. It died in committee without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers with disabilities who are paid less than the federal minimum wage under a special certificate. The bill would immediately bar new certificates and require every existing certificate holder to write an annual, individualized transition plan for each subminimum-wage worker, with the plans posted publicly, and would revoke all remaining certificates six years after enactment [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers with disabilities paid subminimum wages

how_it_helps.text: The bill immediately stops the Department of Labor from issuing any new special certificates authorizing subminimum wages under section 14(c) of the Fair Labor Standards Act [S3].

Employers holding existing certificates could not renew them unless they filed annual individualized assessments of each subminimum-wage worker, identified the disability-related obstacles keeping them from jobs at or above minimum wage, and submitted a transition plan with concrete benchmarks for placing each worker in jobs paying at least minimum wage [S2][S3].

Six years after enactment, the entire special-certificate authority would be repealed and every outstanding certificate revoked, ending legal subminimum pay for workers with disabilities outright [S2][S3].

The assessments and transition plans would be posted publicly on the Department of Labor's website, without personally identifiable information, so the public could see what certificate holders were doing [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers holding special wage certificates — largely sheltered workshops and disability service providers — would lose a legal exemption that lets them pay disabled workers less than minimum wage, and would bear the cost of annual assessments and transition plans for those workers [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Sheltered workshops and disability service providers

drawbacks.text: The bill gives no new funding or services for the transition itself: it requires employers to file plans, but does not guarantee that jobs paying at or above minimum wage will actually be available for each worker when the certificates are revoked six years later [S3].

Critics of phasing out subminimum certificates have long argued that some workers in sheltered workshops could lose their current placements before comparable integrated jobs exist, and that employer-written transition plans are not a substitute for real job placement support — a concern this bill's design (reliance on employer paperwork rather than services funding) does not fully answer [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is straightforward: a worker doing the same job as anyone else would no longer legally be paid below the federal minimum. The honest cost is the transition — employers would need to replace subminimum-wage jobs with real ones, and the bill relies on employer-filed plans and public reporting rather than funding services or guaranteeing placements. Those are manageable design flaws rather than reasons the goal itself is unsound, and the six-year runway was meant to soften the shock.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2017 and referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, which never held a markup or vote, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Gregg Harper (R-MS) introduced the bill on March 7, 2017 [S1][S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce — the only action it ever received [S5].
It attracted 52 cosponsors, 37 Democrats and 15 Republicans, but the committee never considered it and it never came to the House floor [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers holding special wage certificates kept their legal authority to pay workers with disabilities below minimum wage for the life of the 115th Congress, with no new reporting requirements or transition obligations.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Certificate-holding employers kept paying subminimum wages

for.name: Rep. Gregg Harper
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 52 cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: 37 of 194 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, forming the majority of its support.

for.name: 15 of 241 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill alongside the Democratic majority of supporters.

against.name: Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to her committee, which took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan: of 52 cosponsors, 37 were Democrats and 15 were Republicans, with a Republican sponsor — but the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call exists.

industries.industry: Sheltered workshops and disability service providers holding 14(c) certificates
industries.note: These employers' business model depends on a legal exemption to pay workers with disabilities less than the minimum wage. The bill would have ended new certificates immediately, imposed annual transition-plan reporting on existing holders, and revoked all certificates after six years, removing that exemption entirely.

industries.industry: Department of Labor (wage and hour enforcement)
industries.note: The bill would shift Labor's workload: it would stop issuing and eventually revoke certificates while taking on new public reporting of employers' transition plans, and employers that kept paying subminimum wages without meeting the conditions would be deemed in violation of Labor's regulations.
